transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, it’s... I guess it really all started a little while back. You see, my wife’s father, my father-in-law, he moved in with us recently. We had to clear out the whole downstairs guest room, move all my old college boxes into the attic, and reorganize half the house just to fit his bed and his giant recliner in there. It was a massive undertaking. 

And ever since he got settled in, I just... I don’t know, I’m here because I’ve been acting completely out of character. I’ve been snapping at my wife over just the dumbest, littlest house things. The other day she left a damp sponge in the sink and I practically bit her head off about it. I’ve never been like that with her, we usually get along great, but my patience is just gone. 

And on top of that, I’m just... I’m putting off all these jobs and paperwork that I used to stay right on top of. The mail is just piling up on the kitchen island, bills are sitting there unopened, and the gutters need cleaning, and I know I need to do it all, but I just look at the mess and walk away. I can't bring myself to care. 

I try to get some space, you know? I go out to my workshop in the backyard, or I take my gear out to the lake to try and fish—things that usually relax me and give me a breather. But lately, I just can’t seem to get my head quiet. Even when I’m out there staring at the water or trying to work on a project, my brain is just buzzing and spinning about the house and her dad and everything I'm not doing, and I just... I can't turn it off. I can't even enjoy a simple afternoon of fishing anymore. So, she told me I needed to come talk to somebody, and... well, here I am.
Have you had days where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in most things—not just the house or work—but in general—for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Well, let me think about that... hopeless? No, I wouldn't use the word hopeless. I mean, it’s not like I’m just lying in bed all day pulling the covers over my head, giving up on life or anything like that. I still get up every morning at 6:30, just like I always have, I go down and make my coffee—I usually do a French press, it’s just a morning routine I really like to stick to—and I still, you know, want to do things. 

Like I was saying about the fishing, it’s not that I don’t care about fishing anymore. I still look at my rods in the garage and think, man, I'd love to get out on the water today. The interest is absolutely still there. I just... I can't enjoy it because my brain is going a mile a minute about the house and the mess and her dad's giant recliner taking up half the living room. So it’s not that I’ve lost interest in life in general, it’s just that I’m too wound up to actually enjoy the things I am interested in, if that makes sense. 

And it’s definitely not every single day, all day long. Like, just this past Thursday, my wife took her dad to his cardiologist appointment—which is a whole production, let me tell you, getting his heavy walker folded up and wedged into the trunk of her sedan, it barely fits—but anyway, they were gone for about three or four hours, and I felt completely fine! I had the house to myself, it was finally quiet, I put on some classic rock on the stereo, made myself a turkey sandwich, and I felt exactly like my old self. So, no, it’s not this constant, dark depression every day for two weeks. It’s really just... I feel like a pressure cooker when he's around and the house is in chaos, you know? But when I get a real break, I'm okay.

Can you tell me if, besides being irritable, there have been days when you didn't take pleasure in activities that usually make you happy—even things like your morning coffee or working on projects in your workshop?

Well, no, it’s... like I was trying to explain a minute ago, it’s really not that the pleasure is gone. Take my morning coffee, for instance, since you brought that up. I buy these specific beans from a little local roaster downtown—usually a Guatemalan dark roast, because it has this really nice, almost chocolatey finish to it that I just love. When I get up and grind those beans, and I pour the hot water over them in the press, that smell... I mean, I still absolutely love that smell. It makes me happy, just like it always has. I take that first sip and I think, man, that is a great cup of coffee. So the pleasure is definitely still there. It’s not like everything tastes like cardboard or I’m just walking around like a zombie going through the motions. 

And it's the exact same thing with the workshop. I was actually out there just... I think it was Tuesday afternoon? I was sanding down this old oak side table that I picked up at a flea market a couple of months ago, back before everything got so crazy here. I still get a ton of satisfaction out of seeing that old wood grain pop when I wipe away the sawdust. The problem isn't that I don't enjoy the sanding or working with my hands. It's just that while I'm out there trying to do it, I can hear her dad's television blaring through the living room wall because he insists on watching those daytime court shows at maximum volume, and then my jaw clenches up, and I just can't focus on the wood. 

So the actual joy of the project? The feeling of making something look nice again? No, I haven't lost that at all. It's just... it gets completely overshadowed by all this frustration with the house situation, if you see what I mean. I get too distracted by the noise and the mess to stay in the moment. But the actual happiness from those hobbies and routines? No, that's still completely intact. I really haven't lost that.
Have you had days where you felt a noticeable lack of energy or fatigue—like even small tasks felt physically or mentally draining—for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Fatigue? No, I wouldn't say that at all. My energy levels are actually perfectly fine. I mean, I'm 47, so I'm not exactly running triathlons or anything, but I've got plenty of gas in the tank, so to speak. 

Just yesterday, for example, I was out in the yard—we have this massive oak tree in the back, and the leaves just pile up like crazy this time of year—and I spent a solid two, maybe two and a half hours out there raking. Bagged it all up, hauled all those heavy paper bags all the way down the long driveway to the curb. And those things get incredibly heavy when the leaves are damp from the morning dew, let me tell you. But doing all that didn't wear me out physically in the slightest. I came back inside and felt completely fine. 

So it's definitely not that I'm exhausted or dragging myself around the house. And as for the mental side of things, with the small tasks feeling draining... it's really not that I lack the mental energy to do them. Like the mail and the bills I mentioned earlier. It's not that sorting through a few envelopes is exhausting to my brain. I have the energy to sit down and write a check. It's just that I walk into the kitchen, and I see the mail, but I also see his giant plastic pill organizers taking up half the counter space, and I hear that damn TV blaring from the living room again, and my jaw tightens up, and I just get so aggravated that I think, 'To hell with it, I'm not doing this right now.' 

It's not fatigue, it's just... sheer frustration, I guess? I actually almost wish I was tired! Because if I were exhausted, maybe I could just sit in a chair and zone out and ignore the chaos going on around me. But instead, I'm just pacing around, completely wide awake, full of all this nervous energy, just noticing every single little thing that's out of place in my own home. So, no, no lack of energy at all. If anything, I've got too much energy and nowhere productive to put it.
Have you found yourself worrying a lot or having trouble controlling your thoughts about your father-in-law moving in and the changes around the house?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, that is... that’s really the whole reason I’m here talking to you today. Ever since my father-in-law moved in, it’s like I just can't turn my brain off. The thoughts about the house and all the changes, they just loop and loop constantly. 

And it’s affecting everything. I’ve been snapping at my wife over the most ridiculous little house things—like, if a cabinet door is left open an inch, or if she leaves a damp sponge in the sink instead of wringing it out, I just lose my patience completely and bite her head off. Which isn't me, you know? I usually take things in stride. But I'm just so on edge. And because my mind is always racing about the situation, I’m putting off all these jobs and paperwork that I used to stay right on top of. I used to pay every bill the day it came in, logged it in a little ledger I keep in the desk, and now the mail just piles up on the counter next to his giant plastic pill organizers because I just can't bring myself to sit down and focus on it. 

I just can’t seem to get my head quiet. Like I was saying before about the workshop, or when I'm trying to think about going fishing... I’ll go out there to escape, right? I'll be standing there with a piece of sandpaper in my hand, or looking through my tackle box, and instead of relaxing, I'm just stewing. I'm worrying about how much space his recliner is taking up, or if that TV is going to be blaring again when I walk back inside, or how long this whole living arrangement is actually supposed to last. I try to tell myself to just drop it, just look at the wood, just look at the fishing lures, but I can't control it. My mind just keeps racing right back to the house and the mess, no matter how hard I try to shut it off.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms like trouble sleeping, muscle tension, or a racing heart, or felt constantly on edge, especially when thinking about the situation at home?

Physical symptoms? Like a racing heart? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I’m not having panic attacks or clutching my chest or anything extreme. My heart rate is completely normal. I actually checked my blood pressure just the other day at the grocery store—you know those little sit-down machines they have over by the pharmacy waiting area? I sat down in one just to see, because with all this stress with the house, you always hear about guys my age developing heart issues, but it was perfectly fine. It was something like 115 over 75, and my resting heart rate was right around 68. So physically speaking, the ticker is doing just great. 

And as for sleeping, I really don't have any trouble there either. I've always been a very heavy sleeper. Once my head hits the pillow, I am out cold for the night. I have this whole evening routine that works perfectly for me—I usually read a chapter or two of whatever book I'm on. Right now, it's this incredibly detailed biography of Ulysses S. Grant, just a massive hardcover that really gets into the weeds of his early military career out West before the Civil War, which I just find absolutely fascinating. Anyway, I read a few pages of that, my eyes get heavy, and I sleep straight through till morning. It actually helps that her dad usually passes out in his recliner with the TV on by 8:30 or 9:00 PM, so by the time I actually go to bed around 11:00, the house is finally, mercifully quiet. So, no, my sleep hasn't been disrupted in the slightest. 

You mentioned muscle tension... I mean, I know I said earlier that my jaw clenches up when I hear that daytime TV blaring through the walls or when I see his pill organizers taking up my counter space, but it's not like I'm walking around all day with my shoulders tied up in knots, you know? My back doesn't ache, I'm not getting tension headaches, my muscles aren't sore. It's really just that quick, immediate flash of annoyance when the noise or the clutter hits me, rather than some constant physical strain on my body. I’m definitely on edge mentally, like I was saying about how I can’t stop thinking about the mess and how much space he’s taking up, but my body itself feels fine. It’s really just my brain that won't give it a rest.

Do you find yourself worrying about a variety of different things in your life, not just the situation at home, like work, health, or other responsibilities, even when there isn't an immediate problem?

No, not at all. It’s really just this one specific thing. I mean, if you took the current situation at the house out of the equation, I’m probably the least worried guy you’d ever meet. I really don't sit around inventing problems or stressing about things that haven't happened yet. 

Take our finances or daily responsibilities, for example. Since I'm not working right now and I'm the one managing the household day-to-day, I usually keep a very tight ship. I have this whole system—an Excel spreadsheet I built myself, color-coded, where I track every single expense. Normally, every Sunday morning, I sit down with a cup of black coffee, usually around 7:00 AM before anyone else is even awake, and I balance everything out to the penny. We’re in good shape financially, so there's absolutely zero stress there. I don't lose a wink of sleep over money or the economy or what the stock market is doing. 

And health? Like I told you about the blood pressure machine at the grocery store, I keep an eye on things, but I don't obsess over it. I'm 47, I feel good, I eat reasonably well—except for maybe a weakness for those little powdered donuts every now and then, but who doesn't, right? But I'm certainly not sitting around WebMD-ing every little ache and pain or worrying I'm going to drop dead of some rare disease. 

So, no, my mind doesn't wander off into all these different worst-case scenarios about life in general. It’s a very... localized frustration, I guess you'd call it. It’s entirely centered on the four walls of my house and the fact that my space just isn't my own anymore. Honestly, if her dad were to suddenly decide he wanted to move down to a nice retirement community in Florida tomorrow—which, believe me, I have gently suggested more than a few times, they have some beautiful places down near Sarasota—all of this stress would evaporate instantly. I’d be right back to my normal, easygoing self in a heartbeat. So it’s definitely not a general worrying problem, it’s just... well, it's just a 'him' problem.

When you're not thinking about your father-in-law or the situation at home, do you still find yourself losing interest in things you usually enjoy, or does your interest stay consistent as long as those stressors aren’t on your mind?

Oh, if he's not on my mind? No, my interest is exactly the same as it's always been. I don't lose interest in things at all, not one bit. If you take him out of the picture, I'm still the exact same guy with the exact same hobbies. 

Like I was saying before about the woodworking... I still *want* to do it. I still love it. Just last Thursday, actually, my wife had to take him to his podiatrist appointment—which is a whole production, let me tell you, getting him and his walker down the front steps and into the passenger seat of her sedan takes a solid twenty minutes—but anyway, they were going to be gone for at least three hours. And I tell you, the absolute second her car pulled out of the driveway, it was like this massive, heavy cloud just lifted right off the roof of the house. I went straight out to the garage, poured myself a fresh cup of coffee, and got right to work. 

I'm building this birdhouse right now, it's a replica of a Victorian painted lady house, incredibly detailed. I'm talking tiny little cedar shingles for the roof that I'm cutting completely by hand with a coping saw. It takes absolutely forever, but the detail is just incredible when you get it right. And for those three hours they were gone? I was in absolute heaven. I was completely absorbed in what I was doing, sanding down these tiny little trim pieces, whistling along to the classic rock station on my old garage radio. I didn't feel bored or unmotivated or anything like that. I felt great. 

So the interest is definitely still there, 100 percent. It's just that most of the time, I can't actually enjoy those things because my brain is completely hijacked by what's going on inside the house. If I could just get a consistent break from the noise and the clutter and the constant presence of him just... sitting there in the middle of my living room, I'd be perfectly happy doing all my normal stuff. I still have all the drive to do my projects and go out on the lake, it's just that the frustration about the house ruins the actual experience of doing them when he's around. But yeah, if my mind is clear of all that stress? I'm right as rain.

Have you experienced any days where you felt little to no pleasure in *any* activity, even things you usually enjoy, not just when your father-in-law is around or when you're thinking about the house?

No, honestly, I can't say I have. Like I was trying to explain, it’s really just tied to the house and him. If I’m completely removed from the situation, I’m totally fine. I still get a kick out of all the things I normally do. 

Take last Sunday, for example. My buddy Mark—we’ve known each other since community college, actually used to play in a weekend softball league together before my knees decided they'd had enough of that—he called me up and asked if I wanted to head out to the lake. He’s got this great little 18-foot Tracker boat, nothing too flashy, just a reliable aluminum hull with a decent trolling motor up front, which is just perfect for getting into the shallows where the fish like to hide out. 

Anyway, we got out on the water by about 6:00 AM. It was one of those perfect, crisp mornings, you know? The water looked like absolute glass, and there was just this little bit of mist coming off the surface. We had a big thermos of black coffee, a couple of those foil-wrapped breakfast sandwiches we grabbed from the gas station on the way out, and we just sat out there casting lines for about five hours. I caught two really nice largemouth bass, probably three-pounders each, put up a heck of a fight on a light tackle. And I tell you, doctor, I was having the time of my life. I was laughing, joking around with Mark about the old days, just completely in my element. I didn't feel flat or down or unable to enjoy myself at all. I was genuinely, one-hundred-percent happy. 

It wasn't until we were backing the trailer down the ramp to load the boat back up around noon, and my phone buzzed in my pocket... it was my wife asking if I could stop at the pharmacy on the way home to pick up a refill of her dad's water pills. And I swear, the absolute second I read that text, my stomach just completely dropped. All the tension came rushing right back, and the good mood was just gone, like someone flipped a switch. 

But for those five hours on the boat? I was perfectly happy. So, no, there's never a day where I just can't enjoy *anything*. As long as I'm insulated from the situation at home and I don't have a reminder shoved in my face, I'm exactly the same guy I've always been. It's just getting that distance that's the impossible part these days.

doctor.question: Have you found yourself worrying a lot or having trouble controlling your thoughts about your father-in-law moving in and the changes around the house?

target_item.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because ever since my father-in-law moved in, I’ve been snapping at my wife over little house things, putting off jobs and paperwork I used to stay on top of, and I just can’t seem to get my head quiet even when I’m out in the workshop or trying to fish.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about having trouble controlling thoughts and worrying specifically about the father-in-law moving in, which directly matches the patient's manifestation of not being able to get his head quiet in response to the stressor.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. I mean, that is... that’s really the whole reason I’m here talking to you today. Ever since my father-in-law moved in, it’s like I just can't turn my brain off. The thoughts about the house and all the changes, they just loop and loop constantly. 

And it’s affecting everything. I’ve been snapping at my wife over the most ridiculous little house things—like, if a cabinet door is left open an inch, or if she leaves a damp sponge in the sink instead of wringing it out, I just lose my patience completely and bite her head off. Which isn't me, you know? I usually take things in stride. But I'm just so on edge. And because my mind is always racing about the situation, I’m putting off all these jobs and paperwork that I used to stay right on top of. I used to pay every bill the day it came in, logged it in a little ledger I keep in the desk, and now the mail just piles up on the counter next to his giant plastic pill organizers because I just can't bring myself to sit down and focus on it. 

I just can’t seem to get my head quiet. Like I was saying before about the workshop, or when I'm trying to think about going fishing... I’ll go out there to escape, right? I'll be standing there with a piece of sandpaper in my hand, or looking through my tackle box, and instead of relaxing, I'm just stewing. I'm worrying about how much space his recliner is taking up, or if that TV is going to be blaring again when I walk back inside, or how long this whole living arrangement is actually supposed to last. I try to tell myself to just drop it, just look at the wood, just look at the fishing lures, but I can't control it. My mind just keeps racing right back to the house and the mess, no matter how hard I try to shut it off.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced symptoms of anxiety related to the stressor, including physical or cognitive manifestations.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any physical symptoms like trouble sleeping, muscle tension, or a racing heart, or felt constantly on edge, especially when thinking about the situation at home?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical symptoms of anxiety (trouble sleeping, muscle tension, racing heart, feeling on edge), which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Physical symptoms? Like a racing heart? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I’m not having panic attacks or clutching my chest or anything extreme. My heart rate is completely normal. I actually checked my blood pressure just the other day at the grocery store—you know those little sit-down machines they have over by the pharmacy waiting area? I sat down in one just to see, because with all this stress with the house, you always hear about guys my age developing heart issues, but it was perfectly fine. It was something like 115 over 75, and my resting heart rate was right around 68. So physically speaking, the ticker is doing just great. 

And as for sleeping, I really don't have any trouble there either. I've always been a very heavy sleeper. Once my head hits the pillow, I am out cold for the night. I have this whole evening routine that works perfectly for me—I usually read a chapter or two of whatever book I'm on. Right now, it's this incredibly detailed biography of Ulysses S. Grant, just a massive hardcover that really gets into the weeds of his early military career out West before the Civil War, which I just find absolutely fascinating. Anyway, I read a few pages of that, my eyes get heavy, and I sleep straight through till morning. It actually helps that her dad usually passes out in his recliner with the TV on by 8:30 or 9:00 PM, so by the time I actually go to bed around 11:00, the house is finally, mercifully quiet. So, no, my sleep hasn't been disrupted in the slightest. 

You mentioned muscle tension... I mean, I know I said earlier that my jaw clenches up when I hear that daytime TV blaring through the walls or when I see his pill organizers taking up my counter space, but it's not like I'm walking around all day with my shoulders tied up in knots, you know? My back doesn't ache, I'm not getting tension headaches, my muscles aren't sore. It's really just that quick, immediate flash of annoyance when the noise or the clutter hits me, rather than some constant physical strain on my body. I’m definitely on edge mentally, like I was saying about how I can’t stop thinking about the mess and how much space he’s taking up, but my body itself feels fine. It’s really just my brain that won't give it a rest.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient experiences persistent worry or anxiety about multiple areas of life beyond the current home situation, which would help differentiate between Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F43.11).
doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying about a variety of different things in your life, not just the situation at home, like work, health, or other responsibilities, even when there isn't an immediate problem?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about generalized anxiety or worry about a variety of different things (work, health, etc.), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, not at all. It’s really just this one specific thing. I mean, if you took the current situation at the house out of the equation, I’m probably the least worried guy you’d ever meet. I really don't sit around inventing problems or stressing about things that haven't happened yet. 

Take our finances or daily responsibilities, for example. Since I'm not working right now and I'm the one managing the household day-to-day, I usually keep a very tight ship. I have this whole system—an Excel spreadsheet I built myself, color-coded, where I track every single expense. Normally, every Sunday morning, I sit down with a cup of black coffee, usually around 7:00 AM before anyone else is even awake, and I balance everything out to the penny. We’re in good shape financially, so there's absolutely zero stress there. I don't lose a wink of sleep over money or the economy or what the stock market is doing. 

And health? Like I told you about the blood pressure machine at the grocery store, I keep an eye on things, but I don't obsess over it. I'm 47, I feel good, I eat reasonably well—except for maybe a weakness for those little powdered donuts every now and then, but who doesn't, right? But I'm certainly not sitting around WebMD-ing every little ache and pain or worrying I'm going to drop dead of some rare disease. 

So, no, my mind doesn't wander off into all these different worst-case scenarios about life in general. It’s a very... localized frustration, I guess you'd call it. It’s entirely centered on the four walls of my house and the fact that my space just isn't my own anymore. Honestly, if her dad were to suddenly decide he wanted to move down to a nice retirement community in Florida tomorrow—which, believe me, I have gently suggested more than a few times, they have some beautiful places down near Sarasota—all of this stress would evaporate instantly. I’d be right back to my normal, easygoing self in a heartbeat. So it’s definitely not a general worrying problem, it’s just... well, it's just a 'him' problem.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of depression limited to the specific stressor (father-in-law moving in) or if there is a loss of interest in activities independent of the stressor.
doctor.question: When you're not thinking about your father-in-law or the situation at home, do you still find yourself losing interest in things you usually enjoy, or does your interest stay consistent as long as those stressors aren’t on your mind?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a pervasive loss of interest or anhedonia (a symptom of depression) to determine if symptoms extend beyond the specific stressor, which is not covered by the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, if he's not on my mind? No, my interest is exactly the same as it's always been. I don't lose interest in things at all, not one bit. If you take him out of the picture, I'm still the exact same guy with the exact same hobbies. 

Like I was saying before about the woodworking... I still *want* to do it. I still love it. Just last Thursday, actually, my wife had to take him to his podiatrist appointment—which is a whole production, let me tell you, getting him and his walker down the front steps and into the passenger seat of her sedan takes a solid twenty minutes—but anyway, they were going to be gone for at least three hours. And I tell you, the absolute second her car pulled out of the driveway, it was like this massive, heavy cloud just lifted right off the roof of the house. I went straight out to the garage, poured myself a fresh cup of coffee, and got right to work. 

I'm building this birdhouse right now, it's a replica of a Victorian painted lady house, incredibly detailed. I'm talking tiny little cedar shingles for the roof that I'm cutting completely by hand with a coping saw. It takes absolutely forever, but the detail is just incredible when you get it right. And for those three hours they were gone? I was in absolute heaven. I was completely absorbed in what I was doing, sanding down these tiny little trim pieces, whistling along to the classic rock station on my old garage radio. I didn't feel bored or unmotivated or anything like that. I felt great. 

So the interest is definitely still there, 100 percent. It's just that most of the time, I can't actually enjoy those things because my brain is completely hijacked by what's going on inside the house. If I could just get a consistent break from the noise and the clutter and the constant presence of him just... sitting there in the middle of my living room, I'd be perfectly happy doing all my normal stuff. I still have all the drive to do my projects and go out on the lake, it's just that the frustration about the house ruins the actual experience of doing them when he's around. But yeah, if my mind is clear of all that stress? I'm right as rain.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms that meet the criteria for a major depressive episode, specifically persistent anhedonia, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F43.22) over Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood (F43.11).
doctor.question: Have you experienced any days where you felt little to no pleasure in *any* activity, even things you usually enjoy, not just when your father-in-law is around or when you're thinking about the house?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of pleasure or interest in all activities), which is a symptom of depression. My symptom profile only covers adjustment disorder criteria (S081, functional impairment, duration, etc.) and does not include anhedonia.

patient.answer:
No, honestly, I can't say I have. Like I was trying to explain, it’s really just tied to the house and him. If I’m completely removed from the situation, I’m totally fine. I still get a kick out of all the things I normally do. 

Take last Sunday, for example. My buddy Mark—we’ve known each other since community college, actually used to play in a weekend softball league together before my knees decided they'd had enough of that—he called me up and asked if I wanted to head out to the lake. He’s got this great little 18-foot Tracker boat, nothing too flashy, just a reliable aluminum hull with a decent trolling motor up front, which is just perfect for getting into the shallows where the fish like to hide out. 

Anyway, we got out on the water by about 6:00 AM. It was one of those perfect, crisp mornings, you know? The water looked like absolute glass, and there was just this little bit of mist coming off the surface. We had a big thermos of black coffee, a couple of those foil-wrapped breakfast sandwiches we grabbed from the gas station on the way out, and we just sat out there casting lines for about five hours. I caught two really nice largemouth bass, probably three-pounders each, put up a heck of a fight on a light tackle. And I tell you, doctor, I was having the time of my life. I was laughing, joking around with Mark about the old days, just completely in my element. I didn't feel flat or down or unable to enjoy myself at all. I was genuinely, one-hundred-percent happy. 

It wasn't until we were backing the trailer down the ramp to load the boat back up around noon, and my phone buzzed in my pocket... it was my wife asking if I could stop at the pharmacy on the way home to pick up a refill of her dad's water pills. And I swear, the absolute second I read that text, my stomach just completely dropped. All the tension came rushing right back, and the good mood was just gone, like someone flipped a switch. 

But for those five hours on the boat? I was perfectly happy. So, no, there's never a day where I just can't enjoy *anything*. As long as I'm insulated from the situation at home and I don't have a reminder shoved in my face, I'm exactly the same guy I've always been. It's just getting that distance that's the impossible part these days.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms are specifically tied to the stressor of the father-in-law moving in, without generalized anxiety, depression, or physical symptoms. This supports adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22) as the most accurate diagnosis.
